ubo_and_aml_profiling.statutory_law_governance: Canada: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act, SC 2000, c 17 (PCMLTFA) and FINTRAC regulations; Criminal Code, RSC 1985, c C-46 (money-laundering and record-keeping offences); Special Economic Measures Act, SC 1992, c 17; United Nations Act, RSC 1985, c U-2; Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act, SC 2017, c 21. Corporate/UBO: Canada Business Corporations Act, RSC 1985, c C-44 (s. 21.1 et seq., individuals with significant control; Bill C-42 enacting a public beneficial-ownership register); Business Corporations Act (Alberta), RSA 2000, c B-9 (s. 101.1 et seq., ISC register obligations); Alberta corporate registry regime administered by Service Alberta and Red Tape Reduction; FINTRAC guidance on non-financial businesses and money-services-business thresholds.
ubo_and_aml_profiling.ubo_disclosure_level: Government_Only_Access (Alberta ISC registers are internal, disclosed to law enforcement, CRA, FINTRAC and other regulators upon demand; no public Alberta UBO portal as of the relevant evaluation window; federal CBCA entities are transitioning progressively to a publicly accessible register)

ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory real-time screening of all directors, UBOs, authorized signatories and material counterparties against: (a) OFAC SDN List; (b) UN Security Council Consolidated List; (c) Canadian sanctions lists under SEMA, the United Nations Act and the Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act (administered by Global Affairs Canada); (d) FINTRAC and RCMP criminal-finance watchlists. PEPs and high-risk jurisdictions trigger Enhanced Due Diligence with senior-management sign-off. The AdTech SSP/Ad-Exchange platform is classified Low_Risk_Standard for internal AML purposes; however, the SWIFT wire and ACH Direct payment rails impose FINTRAC-derived record-keeping, suspicious-transaction reporting and 5-year retention obligations if the entity crosses money-services-business or money-movement thresholds. Annual re-screening and continuous monitoring are mandatory.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Alberta Corporate Registry (Service Alberta and Red Tape Reduction) — administered through licensed Registry Agents using the NUANS (Newly Upgraded Automated Name Search) system; official access via the authorized agent network and corporate registry services of Service Alberta
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Corporate name must be in English or French (or a combination of both), rendered in the Latin alphabet; non-Latin scripts must be transliterated. The name must include a legal element (Inc., Corp., Incorporated, Limited, Ltd., or the French equivalent) and must be distinguishable from existing registered names, trade names and registered trademarks under Alberta BCA s. 10 and the NUANS search standard.
prohibited_and_sensitive_tokens: Bank / Trust / Trust Company (Bank Act or provincial trust-licensing consent required)
University / College (Ministry of Advanced Education consent required)
Engineer / Engineering (APEGA prior licence or consent required)
Royal (Crown consent in right of Alberta required)
Canada (federal Minister consent required for federal name components)
Municipality / City / County / Regional (municipal consent required)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: Upon name refusal at the NUANS/registry stage: (1) request written reasons from the Registration Officer; (2) file a formal reconsideration with supplementary evidence of distinctiveness (trademark-search results, common-law usage affidavits, domain-name and storefront evidence) within 30 days; (3) if refused again, apply to the Court of King's Bench of Alberta for judicial review / statutory appeal under the Alberta Business Corporations Act, RSA 2000, c B-9, s. 10, by originating application within the applicable limitation window (typically 30 days from the decision); (4) alternatively, re-file a revised name with a new NUANS report and pay the applicable filing fee. Extension of an existing name reservation may be requested at the registry for an additional fee; after final disposition, a fresh NUANS report is required.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Permissible only as a registered-office / registered-agent arrangement with an identifiable physical street address in Alberta at which process can be served during business hours; a P.O. Box is insufficient. A reputable virtual-office or registered-agent address is accepted for a low-risk AdTech SSP, but the Alberta Corporate Registry may reject addresses flagged for mass use by unrelated entities. The corporation must maintain a registered office, and for CRA substantive-review purposes should retain board minutes, a bank account and demonstrable operational substance. Virtual offices are not accepted as a substitute for head-office substance in a tax audit or customs/trade filing context.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low risk: approximately 5% probability in the first operating year for a standard Alberta business corporation. Probability escalates to 10-15% if a FINTRAC AML/CFT review, a CRA corporate tax audit, or a registry integrity inspection of the registered-agent address is triggered. The SSP/Ad-Exchange digital-services model with SWIFT/ACH rails may attract additional scrutiny only where a mass virtual-office address hosts multiple unrelated entities.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Business Corporations Act (Alberta), RSA 2000, c B-9, ss. 9, 12, 14, 18, 105 and 123
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Registrar of Corporations, Alberta Corporate Registry, Service Alberta
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No statutory minimum paid-up share capital is prescribed under the ABCA. The corporation may be incorporated with zero issued shares; shares are issued only for consideration deemed sufficient by the directors. No escrow deposit or paid-up capital placement is required at formation.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLVED, that the corporation ratifies the Articles of Incorporation filed with the Alberta Corporate Registry and adopts Bylaw No. 1; that the share subscription of the incorporator is accepted and 100 common shares are issued for CAD 100; that the registered office be and hereby is established at 1200, 888 4th Avenue SW, Calgary, Alberta T2P 0V5; that the individuals named in the Notice of Directors are elected as the first directors; that the officers designated by the board are authorized to open bank accounts, execute contracts, engage counsel, and complete business number registration; and that directors and officers shall perform all acts necessary to carry on business as a programmatic advertising exchange platform.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry via authorized Registry Agent
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Conduct a NUANS name search for the proposed corporate name. If an exact or confusingly similar name is found, obtain written consent from the holder or select another name. If no name is desired, proceed with a numbered company designation. Submit the name search request through an authorized Alberta Registry Agent or the online Corporate Registry portal; the name reservation is valid for 90 days.
required_dossiers: Written consent of objecting corporation, if applicable
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the name is refused, file an amended reservation with a new proposed name; alternatively, elect to receive a numbered company designation and reserve the name later.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Corporate Counsel / Authorized Alberta Registry Agent
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Draft the Articles of Incorporation, Notice of Registered Office, and Notice of Directors in compliance with the ABCA. Confirm the registered office is a physical street address in Alberta and is not a post office box. Ensure the proposed director slate satisfies Alberta residency requirements, namely at least 25% of directors resident in Canada or, if fewer than four directors, at least one resident Canadian director. Prepare consents to act as directors and set the authorized share structure.
required_dossiers: Consent to Act as Director forms
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: Correct any deficiency identified by counsel or the registry and prepare amended forms for resubmission; no government filing occurs until the full dossier is complete.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Registrar of Corporations, Alberta Corporate Registry
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Submit the executed Articles of Incorporation, Notice of Registered Office, and Notice of Directors to the Alberta Corporate Registry online or by mail. Pay the statutory CAD 200 filing fee. The Registrar will issue a Certificate of Incorporation on approval; the corporation exists on that date.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registrar issues a query or rejection letter, respond with corrected forms within the prescribed period; if the filing lapses, resubmit the Articles with the same fee.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: First Board Meeting and Governance Adoption
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Convene the inaugural board meeting or use unanimous written resolution. Adopt Bylaw No. 1, ratify the Articles of Incorporation, confirm the registered office, issue share certificates for subscribed shares, elect officers, and approve the opening of corporate bank accounts. Record minutes or signed resolution in the corporate records book.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If director residence requirements are not met, the board shall appoint an additional resident Canadian director and file an updated Notice of Directors.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: CRA Business Number and Tax Account Registration
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Canada Revenue Agency - Business Registration Online
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: After receiving the Certificate of Incorporation, register the corporation with the Canada Revenue Agency to obtain a federal Business Number. Register for GST/HST if taxable supplies exceed CAD 30,000 annually or if voluntary registration is desired. Open payroll and corporate income tax accounts as required. Alberta does not impose a provincial sales tax, but Alberta corporate income tax is administered by the CRA for corporations with a permanent establishment in Alberta.
required_dossiers: Notice of Directors and officer information
Banking details for CRA direct debit, if applicable
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If CRA rejects or queries the registration, update the application through My Business Account or CRA Business Registration Online and provide proof of incorporation and director identity.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Annual Return and Continuing Compliance Setup
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry and applicable Municipal Authority
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Set a compliance calendar for the annual return, which Alberta corporations must file within two months after each incorporation anniversary. Confirm the filing fee and current director/officer registry. Obtain a municipal business licence if the corporation maintains a physical office, and secure workers' compensation coverage with Alberta WCB if employees are hired. Maintain the corporate records book in Alberta containing articles, by-laws, minutes, and share registry.
required_dossiers: Municipal business licence application, if applicable
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the corporation is struck from the register for non-filing, apply for restoration under the ABCA and pay all arrears and late fees.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Not applicable — no manufacturing or industrial facility; non-industrial commercial office for AdTech software and platform operations.
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: No regulated operating licence is required for programmatic ad exchange or SSP activities in Alberta.

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Exempt — no EIA or registration is required for a leasehold commercial office under the Environmental Protection and Enhancement Act (EPEA) and the Activities Designation Regulation.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: N/A — no wastewater discharge, VOC emissions, or industrial waste generation; standard municipal solid waste and recycling collection applies; office HVAC emissions remain below applicable air quality thresholds.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Fire and life safety certification per the Alberta Fire Code for office occupancy; WHMIS compliance for any incidental workplace chemicals; Alberta Workers' Compensation Board account clearance if employees are engaged; no structural load inspection is required for standard leasehold office fit-out.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and Revenu Québec for provincial GST/HST administration in Quebec; for Alberta, CRA administers federal GST and Alberta corporate income tax through the My Business Account portal.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: A foreign entity carrying on business in Canada must apply for a CRA Business Number (BN) and register for GST/HST using Form RC1 or the Business Registration Online service. Corporate income tax account registration arises automatically on federal incorporation; an extra-provincial corporation must obtain an Alberta corporate registration through the Corporate Registry and then activate its CRA tax accounts. Non-resident entities may also require a Canadian agent for service and must file prescribed forms with CRA.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: No check-the-box or full pass-through election exists in Canada for corporations; taxation is automatic at the entity level under the Income Tax Act. Available elections relevant to cross-border structures include: GST/HST small-supplier exemption and voluntary registration; section 216 election for non-resident operators claiming net-basis taxation of rents and timber royalties; and treaty-based election documentation to claim reduced withholding under an applicable income tax treaty. Hybrid mismatch rules apply under the Income Tax Act but do not allow the corporation itself to alter its classification.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: GST/HST (Goods and Services Tax / Harmonized Sales Tax)
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 (i.e., taxable revenues exceed CAD 30,000 in any single calendar quarter or over the preceding four consecutive calendar quarters; the threshold applies to worldwide taxable supplies for non-resident registrants unless a mandatory registration arises from carrying on business in Canada).
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Canada does not impose mandatory real-time electronic invoice clearance or digital stamping. CRA accepts electronically issued and retained invoices where they satisfy the Excise Tax Act record-keeping and documentary requirements. GST/HST returns must be filed electronically via GST/HST NETFILE, Extranet File Transfer, or approved EDI when annual taxable supplies exceed CAD 1,000,000; records supporting zero-rated exports must be retained for six years.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Zero-rating is available under Schedule VI to the Excise Tax Act for supplies of goods exported by the supplier, and for services supplied to a non-resident purchaser where the services are supplied for use wholly outside Canada. The supplier must have WTO evidence of export such as export documentation, shipping records, and payment terms showing the goods left Canada or the services were delivered outside Canada. A GST/HST-registered non-resident can claim input tax credits and net refunds on export operations.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Declaration (CBSA eManifest or equivalent export reporting documentation)
Bill of Lading or Airway Bill evidencing shipment to the foreign destination
Commercial Invoice, sale contract, and related export transaction records
Inward Remittance Certificate or equivalent wire/ACH/SWIFT payment evidence establishing consideration received
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: CRA may reassess zero-rated export claims, disallow input tax credits, and recover GST/HST together with interest. Civil penalties for false or misleading export statements may be levied under subsection 285.1 of the Excise Tax Act at 25% of the claimed amount, and willful evasion carries criminal prosecution exposure under the Excise Tax Act and Income Tax Act. Export substantiation records must be preserved for six years; failure to produce them on assessment triggers retroactive clawback and interest.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada) — central monetary and currency authority; prudential banking and foreign-exchange supervision administered by the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI); anti-money-laundering supervision by the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC) under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (PCMLTFA).
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: Canada maintains a wholly free-floating, fully convertible currency regime; no exchange-control legislation restricts current-account or capital-account flows. Dividend and profit remittances from an Alberta Business Corporation to non-resident shareholders are unrestricted from an FX standpoint but are subject to Income Tax Act (Can.) Part XIII withholding (domestic 25%, generally treaty-reduced to 15% or 5% for US corporate shareholders under the Canada-US Income Tax Convention). Capital repatriation by redemption of share capital is permitted subject only to ABCA solvency tests, without central-bank approval.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: Not applicable — Canada imposes no surrender, conversion timeline, or repatriation interval for export or service receipts. Foreign-currency proceeds (USD, EUR, or otherwise) derived from programmatic advertising services may be retained freely in any currency; the only statutory reporting is FINTRAC cross-border transaction reporting above CAD 10,000 and standard IFRS disclosure.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.bank_name: Royal Bank of Canada (RBC Royal Bank)
tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Operational Account and Capital Escrow Account (multi-currency CAD/USD)
Operational Account and Share-Subscription Trust Account
Operational Account (CAD/USD) with integrated FX hedging desk

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.bank_name: Bank of Montreal (BMO Bank of Montreal)
tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Operational Account (CAD/USD) and Capital Escrow Account
Operational Account (CAD) with provincial treasury acceleration

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Medium — suitable for low-value ancillary payouts, not primary treasury custody. Canada does not recognise the EU/UK EMI passport; non-resident payment institutions must correspond through a Schedule I bank or register as an MSB/FMSB with FINTRAC before offering remittance services to Canadian residents. The Alberta Corporation may lawfully hold balances at a non-resident EMI (e.g., Wise, Payoneer) for small publisher settlements, but such balances are not CDIC-insured, carry bank de-risking risk, and every foreign payment account must be disclosed to the primary Canadian banker under its AML monitoring framework.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Neither the Bank Act nor the PCMLTFA requires a physical appearance by directors; however, major Schedule I commercial desks generally require a live video interview of at least one Authorised Signatory and the sole director (or a designated officer), with government-issued photo ID. Fully remote opening is available through RBC and BMO commercial portals when beneficial-owner attestations are notarised by a Canadian lawyer/notary; TD and CIBC commonly demand an in-branch appointment in Calgary or Edmonton for first-time non-resident directors. Recommended path: in-branch onboarding at the Calgary Financial Centre (RBC or Scotiabank) supplemented by apostilled corporate records and notarised passport copies.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: High-volume cross-border disbursements to numerous non-face-to-face publishers and ad networks, creating a payment-pattern red flag
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Master Services Agreement and insertion orders; publisher KYC file containing beneficial-owner register, payment wallet/IBAN and tax identification; flow-of-funds map; 3-month transaction ledger sample; anti-fraud policy; sanctions-screening logs of all destination accounts; signed data-protection and AML covenant package.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Source-of-funds opacity on inbound DSP deposits from thinly capitalised US holding entities or intermediated structures
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Group organisational chart; audited/compiled financial statements of the remitting counterparty; bank reference letter from its principal institution; commercial explanation of each intermediary; board minutes adopting the treasury policy; certificate of incumbency and Alberta corporate registry extract.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: FX and settlement activity volume exceeding CAD 1,000,000 per month, inconsistent with a standard SME treasury profile
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: 12-month cash-flow forecast with reconciled accounts; board-approved FX hedging policy; ISDA Master Agreement and credit support annex; digital advertising invoice set; IFRS cash-flow statement and revenue reconciliation.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: OFAC sanctions intersection due to global programmatic supply chain touching restricted-jurisdiction traffic
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: IP geolocation filter logs; contractual representations and warranties from SSP/DSP vendors excluding sanctioned traffic; monthly compliance attestations; generated OFAC/sanctions screening reports in a format acceptable to the bank compliance team.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Routing: SWIFT MT103 wire from the investor bank to the Alberta entity's CAD/USD Operational or Share-Subscription account at a Schedule I bank, with Remittance Information (field 70) citing 'SHARE CAPITAL CONTRIBUTION — CA_CORP — CA_AB' and the subscription resolution reference. No Bank of Canada or OSFI approval is required for inbound equity; however, the receiving bank will require a corporate resolution, share subscription agreement, source-of-funds attestation, and beneficial-owner verification of all 10% shareholders. For wires exceeding USD 100,000, provide a statutory declaration and compiled financial statements of the investor to meet enhanced due-diligence standards. Investment Canada Act (ICA) notification is generally not required for greenfield incorporation; a status declaration confirming no Canadian business acquisition is included in the banking packet.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Primary rails for ad exchange payouts: (1) SWIFT MT103 with ISO 20022 purpose codes (e.g., 'SAPA' for digital services) for high-value cross-border settlements; interbank settlement via Lynx (CAD) and Fedwire/CHIPS (USD) through correspondent networks; (2) ACH Batch / Automated Funds Transfer for low-value domestic CAD disbursements; (3) same-day EFT Credit for urgent Canadian vendor settlements. Commercial Letters of Credit (UCP600) are not a customary rail for recurring digital service fees; a Standby LC or bank guarantee is the only trade-security instrument practicable if a publisher mandates one. Every outbound instruction carries a unique transaction reference (UTR) to support FINTRAC reconciliation and straight-through processing.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Outright deliverable FX forwards in USD/CAD and EUR/CAD under an ISDA 1998 FX forward master agreement
FX swaps (spot versus forward rollovers) for settlement timing alignment
Cross-currency interest rate swaps (XCCY) for USD/CAD structural treasury management
Vanilla FX options (European-style call/put with premium) on USD/CAD and EUR/CAD

Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) — legally permissible in Canada, but non-standard for CAD given full convertibility; recommended only when the counterparty's jurisdiction imposes a restricted-currency overlay

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late fee CAD 200 (USD 148); administrative dissolution after two consecutive years of non-filing

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Federal Annual Return under CBCA (only if federally incorporated)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Corporations Canada (Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 60 days after the anniversary of the corporation's incorporation
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late fee CAD 100 (USD 74); possible dissolution after two consecutive years of non-filing

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No mandatory audit for a non-distributing private corporation if unanimous shareholders' consent waives the auditor annually; mandatory audit required for any distributing or offering corporation under securities law, or upon shareholder demand by holders of 5% or more of voting shares under the Alberta Business Corporations Act
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: IFRS for public or distributing corporations; ASPE (Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises) for private enterprises

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: Alberta corporations must maintain an Individual with Significant Control (ISC) register identifying any individual owning 25% or more of shares or exercising comparable control; the register is not filed annually but must be updated continuously and share transfers triggering ISC changes recorded within 15 days

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: Federal general corporate income tax rate: 15%. Alberta general corporate income tax rate: 8%. Combined general rate: 23%. Federal small-business rate: 9%. Alberta small-business rate: 2%. Combined eligible Canadian-controlled private corporation small-business rate: 11%, generally applicable to qualifying active business income within the applicable small-business limits.
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: A qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporation may claim the federal small-business deduction on up to CAD 500,000 of qualifying active business income, subject to the associated-corporation and taxable-capital phase-out rules. Alberta generally provides a CAD 500,000 small-business limit at a 2% provincial rate. The federal general rate may be reduced by the 13% general rate reduction for qualifying income. Canadian-controlled private corporations may qualify for refundable and non-refundable scientific research and experimental development incentives where statutory requirements are met. The capital cost allowance system, immediate expensing rules where available, and clean-technology or other targeted investment tax credits may reduce taxable income or tax payable. No general corporate tax holiday applies to an Alberta advertising technology corporation solely because it operates in Alberta.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: Federal T2 Corporation Income Tax Return, filed electronically through CRA-approved tax software under the Corporation Internet Filing program. Alberta AT1 Alberta Corporate Income Tax Return is generally filed electronically through the CRA corporate tax filing process or an approved filing system.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual return; corporate instalments generally monthly, or quarterly where the corporation satisfies the applicable instalment conditions.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: The T2 and AT1 returns are due six months after the end of each taxation year. Any remaining balance is generally due two months after year-end. A qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporation may generally pay the balance three months after year-end if the statutory conditions are met, including the applicable taxable-income threshold and association rules.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Legal name, business number, taxation year start and end dates, corporation type, province of permanent establishment, incorporation details, and whether the corporation is resident in Canada.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident corporation carrying on business in Canada must identify its Canadian permanent establishment and file a T2 for the Canadian tax year. A corporation resident in Canada is generally taxable on worldwide income, subject to treaty relief and foreign tax credit rules.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Information concerning associated Canadian-controlled private corporations and allocation of the federal business limit.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Disclose foreign and Canadian control, ownership, associated corporations, and business-limit allocations accurately. Non-resident ownership can prevent CCPC status even where the corporation is incorporated in Canada.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Reconciliation of accounting net income or loss to income for tax purposes, including non-deductible expenses, timing differences, reserves, depreciation, and other tax adjustments.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Exclude accounting expenses that are not deductible under the Income Tax Act. Intercompany management fees, platform fees, royalties, and financing costs require support for business purpose, reasonableness, withholding, and transfer-pricing compliance.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Capital cost allowance by class, additions, dispositions, undepreciated capital cost, and recapture or terminal loss.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Identify Canadian depreciable property used in the Canadian business. Software, servers, equipment, leasehold improvements, and acquired intellectual property must be classified under the applicable capital-cost-allowance rules.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Calculation of the federal small-business deduction for qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporations.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Do not claim the deduction unless the corporation satisfies CCPC, active-business, associated-corporation, taxable-capital, and specified-investment-business conditions.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Shareholder information for persons or entities owning specified voting or equity interests, as required by the return.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Report foreign corporate and individual shareholders and maintain beneficial-ownership records. Shareholder information must be consistent with corporate registers and beneficial-ownership filings.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Part XIII tax and other information relating to amounts paid or credited to non-residents, where applicable.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Apply withholding before payment or credit of taxable Canadian-source amounts. Treaty reductions require beneficial ownership, residence, eligibility, and anti-avoidance analysis; retain supporting forms and certificates.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Information concerning transfers or loans to non-resident trusts, where applicable.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Review whether advertising revenue, intellectual property, cash, or other property has been transferred or loaned to a non-resident trust. File only where the statutory conditions are met.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Information for corporations that were non-resident or deemed non-resident, including treaty-residence and permanent-establishment matters.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Disclose treaty residence, Canadian permanent establishment, branch operations, and relevant treaty positions. A corporation cannot rely on incorporation alone to establish treaty residence.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Federal foreign tax credits for foreign business income and non-business income.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Claim only foreign income or withholding taxes that are legally imposed, paid, attributable to foreign income, and supported by evidence. Coordinate the claim with foreign tax deductions and treaty limitations.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Investment tax credit calculations, including SR&ED and other qualifying expenditures where applicable.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For an AdTech platform, distinguish qualifying technological research from ordinary software development, maintenance, marketing, and commercial deployment. Maintain project-level technical and expenditure records.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Form T106, Information Return of Non-Arm's Length Transactions with Non-Residents, for reportable transactions with non-resident related parties.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Report material payments, receipts, loans, financing, royalties, advertising services, data services, software licenses, and other non-arm's-length transactions. The T106 reporting threshold is generally based on the total reportable non-arm's-length transactions with a non-resident, including relevant receivables and payables, exceeding CAD 1 million in the reporting period.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Information Return Relating to Controlled and Not-Controlled Foreign Affiliates, where the corporation owns or is deemed to own a foreign affiliate.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: File for relevant foreign subsidiaries or affiliates and analyze foreign accrual property income, exempt surplus, taxable surplus, capital gains, and repatriation consequences.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Foreign Income Verification Statement for specified foreign property exceeding the statutory cost threshold.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Generally required where specified foreign property exceeds CAD 100,000 at any time in the year. Foreign bank accounts, securities, receivables, and certain foreign intellectual-property interests may be relevant; exclude property used exclusively in an active business.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Alberta taxable income reconciliation and Alberta corporate tax computation.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Allocate income to Alberta and other jurisdictions using the applicable Canadian provincial allocation rules. Revenue from users, advertisers, exchanges, or affiliates outside Alberta does not automatically constitute Alberta taxable income.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Alberta small-business deduction and associated-corporation allocation, where applicable.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Claim only for an eligible CCPC and qualifying active business income. Verify federal and Alberta associated-corporation calculations separately.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Monthly or quarterly corporate income tax instalments based on the corporation's estimated current-year liability or permitted prior-year alternatives.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A foreign-owned Canadian corporation must calculate instalments using Canadian taxable income and Canadian corporate tax, not the parent's consolidated tax estimate.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing of a T2 generally attracts a penalty of 5% of the unpaid balance plus 1% of the unpaid balance for each complete month late, up to 12 months. Where a demand to file has been issued or a prior late-filing penalty applied, the enhanced penalty can generally be 10% plus 2% per complete month, up to 20 months. Alberta may impose corresponding provincial late-filing consequences. Interest on unpaid tax, instalments, penalties, and certain remittances is compounded daily at the prescribed rate. Repeated or grossly negligent failures may trigger gross-negligence penalties, reassessments, audit, and prosecution.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: T4A, T4, NR4, and related CRA information returns, filed electronically through CRA Web Forms, Internet file transfer, or approved payroll and information-return software, depending on the payment type.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual information returns; payroll remittances generally monthly or more frequently depending on remitter status.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Most annual information returns are due by the last day of February following the calendar year. NR4 slips and returns are generally due by the last day of March following the calendar year. Payroll source deductions are due according to the assigned remitter schedule.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Gross amount paid or credited to a non-resident and the corresponding Part XIII tax withheld.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Use the appropriate income code for dividends, interest, royalties, management fees, or other taxable Canadian-source amounts. Report the gross amount even where a treaty rate reduces the tax.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Beneficial-owner declarations supporting reduced Part XIII withholding for individuals, corporations, or partnerships.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Obtain and retain the applicable declaration before applying a treaty rate. The payer remains responsible for reasonable verification and cannot rely on a nominal recipient where beneficial ownership is doubtful.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Payments to Canadian residents for services, employment, commissions, or other reportable amounts.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Classify employees, contractors, agencies, and platform participants correctly. Misclassification can create source-deduction, CPP, EI, payroll-tax, and permanent-establishment exposure.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late or incorrect information returns may attract fixed penalties based on the number of slips and the period of delay. Failure to deduct or remit Part XIII tax can result in assessment of the unremitted tax, interest, penalties, and potential director liability. Gross negligence or intentional false reporting can result in prosecution.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: The domestic Canadian Part XIII withholding rate on taxable dividends paid or credited to a non-resident is 25%. A treaty commonly reduces the rate to 5% for a qualifying corporate shareholder meeting the ownership and limitation conditions and to 15% in other qualifying cases. Under the Canada-United States treaty, the principal rates are generally 5% for a qualifying direct corporate shareholder and 15% otherwise. Treaty entitlement must be assessed at the payment date.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: The Canadian payer must determine whether the recipient is resident in a treaty country, the beneficial owner of the income, entitled to treaty benefits, and not denied benefits under limitation-on-benefits, principal-purpose, anti-conduit, or comparable anti-abuse rules. Obtain a valid NR301 declaration for a corporate beneficial owner, NR302 for a partnership, or NR303 for another entity before applying a reduced dividend, interest, or royalty rate where appropriate. A tax-residency certificate should be obtained from the recipient's tax authority when residence is material or requested by the CRA. The payer must retain ownership charts, treaty analysis, contracts, certificates, declarations, payment records, and evidence of beneficial ownership. Remit withheld tax to the CRA by the 15th day of the month following the month of payment or credit, file the applicable NR4 information return, and issue NR4 slips. Treaty relief does not eliminate the obligation to withhold unless the treaty or domestic exemption clearly applies.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: The domestic Part XIII rate is generally 25% on royalties and interest paid or credited to non-residents. Treaty rates vary by treaty and income category. Many Canadian treaties reduce royalty withholding to rates commonly ranging from 0% to 15%, depending on the type of royalty and recipient. Ordinary arm's-length interest is exempt from Canadian withholding under many treaties, including the Canada-United States treaty, but exceptions can apply to participating debt, contingent interest, related-party interest, and other specified categories. Non-arm's-length interest may be subject to treaty limits or domestic withholding. Software, data, platform access, trademarks, algorithms, customer lists, and advertising technology payments must be classified by legal rights and substance; a service fee is not automatically a royalty. Management and technical service fees require separate treaty and domestic-source analysis.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: Canadian contemporaneous transfer-pricing documentation is generally required under Income Tax Act section 247(4) for non-arm's-length cross-border transactions. A formal documentation exemption generally applies where the corporation and associated corporations have gross revenues of less than CAD 10 million for the year, subject to the statutory rules. The CAD 10 million threshold does not eliminate the arm's-length pricing requirement, T106 reporting, or the need to support material transactions. Canada generally does not impose a universal OECD-style Local File and Master File requirement for every taxpayer. Country-by-Country reporting generally applies to a Canadian-resident ultimate parent or surrogate parent of an MNE group with consolidated group revenue of at least EUR 750 million in the preceding fiscal year. A qualifying Canadian-resident constituent entity may have notification and filing obligations where the group threshold is met.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Canada has no standalone United Arab Emirates-style Economic Substance Regulations regime. Economic substance is nevertheless relevant under the Income Tax Act, the transfer-pricing rules, the general anti-avoidance rule, treaty anti-abuse principles, beneficial-ownership analysis, foreign-affiliate rules, and permanent-establishment analysis. A Canadian AdTech corporation should maintain Canadian decision-making, personnel, technology functions, risk control, contractual authority, records, and operational capacity consistent with the profits allocated to Canada. A principal company that contracts with an Alberta corporation while the Alberta entity performs the key platform, sales, data, or risk functions may face a transfer-pricing adjustment, withholding challenge, or permanent-establishment dispute.
required_transfer_pricing_controls: Prepare a functional analysis covering functions, assets, and risks for the DSP, SSP, exchange, data, sales, engineering, and payment activities.
Delineate the actual transactions rather than relying solely on intercompany agreement labels.
Benchmark platform service fees, technology licenses, data fees, advertising inventory arrangements, financing, and cost-sharing charges using reliable comparables.
Document revenue recognition, gross-versus-net agency analysis, advertiser and publisher settlement flows, fraud losses, chargebacks, rebates, and platform fees.
Reconcile transfer-pricing policies to the T2, T106, financial statements, GST/HST records, and customs or payment records where relevant.
Review withholding tax on royalties, interest, management fees, and technical services before payment or credit.
Monitor year-end true-ups and ensure that corresponding adjustments, debit notes, and treaty procedures are legally supportable.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Tax Evasion and False Tax Reporting
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Knowingly concealing advertising revenue, fabricating expenses, diverting platform fees to an offshore affiliate, using false invoices, or making materially false statements in a T2, AT1, T106, or information return.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under Income Tax Act section 239, conviction can result in a fine of 50% to 200% of the tax sought to be evaded, imprisonment for up to two years, or both, in addition to reassessment, tax, interest, and civil penalties. Gross-negligence penalties are generally 50% of the understated tax or overstated credit.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and officers may face criminal liability where they personally participated, authorized, assented to, or acquiesced in the offence. Corporate status does not protect an individual from prosecution. Travel restrictions are not an automatic tax sanction but may arise through criminal process, bail, arrest, or a court order.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Failure to File or Failure to Comply
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failure to file the T2, AT1, T106, T1134, T1135, NR4, or other required return; failure to respond to a CRA demand; or failure to provide books, records, or requested information.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Late-filing penalties, failure-to-file penalties, daily prescribed interest, compliance orders, prosecution, and potential fines apply. Failure to comply with a demand to file or provide information can constitute a separate offence under the Income Tax Act.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be prosecuted for directing or consenting to non-compliance. Personal assessment is not automatic for ordinary corporate income tax, but directors may be assessed under specific statutory provisions, including source-deduction and GST/HST director-liability rules.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Unremitted Payroll, GST/HST, or Part XIII Withholding
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failing to withhold or remit payroll deductions, GST/HST, or tax on dividends, interest, royalties, management fees, or other taxable amounts paid to non-residents.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The corporation may be assessed for the unremitted amount, interest, late-remittance penalties, gross-negligence penalties, and prosecution. Part XIII withholding failures can result in liability for the tax that should have been withheld even where the non-resident recipient received the full payment.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors can be personally assessed under Income Tax Act section 227.1 for unremitted source deductions and under applicable GST/HST provisions, subject to statutory due-diligence defenses and limitation periods. Personal bankruptcy does not necessarily eliminate these liabilities.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Charging non-arm's-length royalties, platform fees, data fees, financing costs, or service charges that shift Canadian profit without functional support, or failing to maintain contemporaneous documentation.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The CRA may make a primary adjustment under section 247, impose a 10% transfer-pricing penalty on the adjustment where the statutory threshold is met and documentation requirements are not satisfied, assess interest, and deny unsupported deductions. A corresponding adjustment is not automatic.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors generally face corporate assessment rather than automatic personal assessment, but intentional manipulation, false records, or participation in evasion can produce criminal and civil exposure.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Routing dividends, interest, or royalties through a conduit entity lacking beneficial ownership, using an inaccurate NR301 declaration, treaty shopping, or applying a reduced rate without confirming residence and treaty entitlement.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The payer may be assessed for the full 25% Part XIII tax, interest, penalties, and information-return failures. Treaty benefits may be denied under domestic anti-avoidance rules, treaty limitation-on-benefits provisions, or principal-purpose tests.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and officers may be personally exposed where they knowingly approved false declarations or deliberate withholding failures. Civil restitution is generally through tax assessments; imprisonment requires applicable criminal conduct and conviction.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Using an Alberta corporation as a nominal contracting entity while foreign personnel habitually conclude contracts, control customer relationships, operate the exchange, or perform core platform functions in Canada or another jurisdiction without corresponding tax reporting.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Possible Canadian or foreign permanent-establishment assessments, corporate income tax, withholding tax, GST/HST, interest, penalties, payroll assessments, and treaty disputes. Contract labels do not override the factual permanent-establishment analysis.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may face personal exposure for knowing participation in fraudulent records or evasion. Ordinary permanent-establishment errors generally create corporate tax exposure rather than automatic imprisonment or travel bans.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Shell Company, Nominee Ownership, and Beneficial-Ownership Concealment
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Maintaining an Alberta corporation with no genuine management, personnel, records, assets, or commercial purpose while using nominee shareholders, undisclosed controllers, or circular transactions to conceal the beneficial owner.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Potential corporate-law penalties, tax reassessment, denial of treaty benefits, anti-avoidance application, money-laundering investigation, and prosecution for false statements or fraud. Canadian corporations must maintain accurate corporate records and comply with applicable beneficial-ownership transparency obligations.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may face civil claims, regulatory orders, fines, disqualification, and criminal liability for fraud or false filings. Travel bans and imprisonment are not automatic and require the applicable enforcement process.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Processing suspicious advertising payments, knowingly dealing with criminal proceeds, structuring payments, disguising beneficial ownership, or failing to file required suspicious transaction reports where the corporation is a reporting entity.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act can impose administrative monetary penalties, compliance orders, and criminal sanctions. Maximum administrative penalties can reach CAD 1 million for an individual and CAD 4 million for an entity, depending on the violation and statutory classification. Criminal proceeds offences can result in significant fines and imprisonment.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Individuals who direct, authorize, consent to, or participate in laundering or terrorist-financing conduct may face prosecution, asset restraint, forfeiture, fines, and imprisonment. A DSP or SSP is not automatically a FINTRAC reporting entity solely because it processes ordinary advertising payments, but its actual payment, remittance, foreign-exchange, or virtual-currency activities must be reviewed.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Deleting bid logs, altering advertiser or publisher settlement data, failing to preserve invoices and contracts, commingling client funds, or maintaining records that cannot substantiate gross revenue, deductions, refunds, fraud losses, or related-party charges.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The CRA may impose penalties, disallow deductions, assess tax using indirect methods, issue requirements to produce information, and prosecute obstruction or destruction of records. Required books and records generally must be retained for the statutory retention period, commonly six years from the end of the relevant year.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and officers may face prosecution for obstruction, destruction of records, or false books. Civil liability may include tax restitution, penalties, and damages; imprisonment and travel restrictions require separate criminal or judicial proceedings.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Paying dividends, management fees, or shareholder loans while insolvent, while source deductions or GST/HST remain unpaid, or without sufficient corporate-law solvency and capital records.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Improper distributions may be recoverable under Alberta or federal corporate law, and shareholder loans or benefits may create taxable income. Unpaid trust amounts can trigger statutory assessments and priority claims.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may face repayment claims, oppression remedies, breach-of-duty claims, and statutory source-deduction or GST/HST assessments. Personal liability depends on the specific statute, conduct, diligence, and limitation period.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Using personal data without lawful authority, falsifying consent or opt-out records, transmitting commercial electronic messages without required consent, or making deceptive advertising representations.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Potential enforcement under Canadian federal and provincial privacy, anti-spam, consumer-protection, and competition laws, including administrative monetary penalties, injunctions, damages, compliance orders, and reputational loss. These liabilities can affect tax deductibility, platform contracts, and regulatory risk assessments.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be personally liable for knowing participation, authorization, or statutory offences where the applicable legislation provides. Tax authorities may challenge payments arising from unlawful or unsupported activities.
